Problem 1: Algorithms
Problem Statement
Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Prove that G possesses a unique minimum spanning tree
if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied: (1) For every partition of the
vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight connecting the two subsets is
unique. (2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight is unique.
Solution
Theorem 1. Let G be an edge-weighted graph. Then G possesses a unique minimum span-
ning tree if and only if both of the following properties are satisfied:
(1) For every partition of the vertex set of G into two subsets, the edge of minimum weight
connecting the two subsets is unique.
(2) For every cycle contained in G, the edge with the maximum weight is unique.
Proof. We prove both directions separately.
(⇒) Uniqueness implies both properties:
Suppose G has a unique minimum spanning tree T.
Proof of Property (1): Suppose for contradiction that there exists a partition (S, V \S) of
the vertex set and two distinct edges e1, e2 both having the same minimum weight w among
all edges crossing this cut.
Since T is a minimum spanning tree, by the fundamental cut property of MSTs, T must
contain at least one minimum-weight edge crossing the cut (S, V \ S).
Without loss of
generality, suppose e1 ∈T.
Since T is a tree, e1 is a bridge in T, meaning that removing e1 disconnects T into exactly
two components. These components must be precisely S and V \ S (as e1 connects these
two sets).
Now consider T ′ = T −{e1} + {e2}. Since e2 also connects S and V \ S, the graph T ′ is
connected and has |V | −1 edges, hence T ′ is a spanning tree.
Furthermore, since w(e1) = w(e2) = w, we have:

Proof of Property (2): Suppose for contradiction that there exists a cycle C in G con-
taining two distinct edges e1, e2 that both have the maximum weight w among all edges in
C.
Case 1: Both e1, e2 ∈T. Then T contains both edges of the cycle C. Since T is a tree,
T is acyclic, so T cannot contain all edges of any cycle. Therefore T does not contain all
edges of C. However, if T contains e1 and e2, and there is a path in C from an endpoint
of e1 to an endpoint of e2 using other edges of C, this would create a cycle in T, which is
impossible.
More precisely: both e1 and e2 are in C, and C is a cycle. If both are in the tree T, then
since T is a tree, there is a unique path in T between any two vertices. But C provides two
distinct paths between the endpoints of e1 (one using e1 and one using e2), so if both edges
are in T, we have a cycle in T, contradiction.

Therefore w(f) = w(e1), which means w(T ′) = w(T), so T ′ is also an MST with T ′ ̸= T,

Thus property (2) must hold.
(⇐) Both properties imply uniqueness:
Suppose properties (1) and (2) both hold. Let T and T ′ be two minimum spanning trees
of G. We will show that T = T ′.
Suppose for contradiction that T ̸= T ′. Then there exists an edge e ∈T \ T ′ (or by
symmetry, an edge in T ′ \ T).
Since e ∈T and T is a tree, removing e from T partitions the vertex set into two
non-empty components, say S and V \ S, where e connects these two sets.
By property (1), there exists a unique minimum-weight edge crossing the cut (S, V \ S).
Since T is an MST and e ∈T crosses this cut, by the cut property of MSTs, e must be
a minimum-weight edge crossing this cut. By property (1), e is the unique such edge.
Now, since T ′ is also an MST, by the cut property, T ′ must contain at least one minimum-
weight edge crossing the cut (S, V \ S). By the uniqueness guaranteed by property (1), this
edge must be e.
Therefore e ∈T ′, contradicting our assumption that e ∈T \ T ′.
This contradiction shows that T \ T ′ = ∅, i.e., T ⊆T ′.
By a symmetric argument
(considering an edge in T ′ \ T if one exists), we also get T ′ ⊆T.
